label: Ceramic Capacitor
description:
**What it is**: A small, non-polarized capacitor used for local energy storage and noise filtering. It stabilizes supply rails and smooths fast changes in current near a chip.

**How it behaves**:
• Stores charge: Q = C·V; more capacitance (C) stores more charge at a given voltage (V).  
• Impedance falls as frequency rises until a minimum, then rises (due to internal inductance).  
• Real parts have internal resistance and inductance, and a maximum voltage rating.  
• Dielectrics: C0G/NP0 (very stable, lower values), X7R/X5R (higher values but lose capacitance under direct-current bias).

**How to use it (decoupling basics)**:
• Place one small ceramic (commonly 0.1 µF) **at each power pin** of a chip; keep the loop (pin → capacitor → ground) as short as possible.  
• Add a nearby larger ceramic (1–10 µF) per rail for local bulk.  
• Choose a voltage rating with comfortable margin (≈2× the rail).  
• Check that effective capacitance under bias is still enough (higher-value, bigger packages drop more).  
• Prefer a direct via to the ground plane next to the capacitor pad.

**Example in practice**:
A 3.3 V microcontroller with four power pins: place one 0.1 µF ceramic at each pin and one 4.7 µF ceramic near the device or regulator output. Keep traces short; one ground via per decoupler.

**Common mistakes**:
• Putting one shared capacitor far from the pins.  
• Using only electrolytics for fast decoupling (they’re too inductive).  
• Choosing a part with a voltage rating too close to the rail.  
• Ignoring capacitance loss under bias and temperature.

**Why it matters**:
Good ceramic decoupling prevents resets, data errors, and noise by supplying fast bursts of current locally and keeping the rail voltage steady.

**Bottom line**: Use small ceramics at each power pin, a larger ceramic per rail, short loops to ground, and adequate voltage and effective capacitance margins.

label: Silicon Diode
description:
**What it is**: A two-terminal part that conducts mainly in one direction. Used for protection, rectification, and steering currents.

**How it behaves**:
• Forward drop ≈ 0.6–0.8 V at rated current (varies with current and temperature).  
• Blocks reverse voltage up to its rating; small reverse leakage still flows.  
• Real parts have current and reverse-voltage limits; switching speed varies by type.

**How to use it**:
• Orientation matters: the banded end is the cathode (current flows from anode → cathode when forward-biased).  
• Choose reverse-voltage rating comfortably above worst-case (≥2× the rail is a safe start).  
• Check power: P ≈ I · V_forward; ensure package can dissipate it.  
• For inductive loads (relays, motors), place a diode across the coil (cathode to supply) to provide a flyback path.  
• For reverse-polarity protection, use a series diode (simple but loses V_forward) or consider a MOSFET “ideal diode” later.

**Example in practice**:
Protect a 12 V relay coil: place a general diode across the coil, cathode to +12 V, anode to the transistor side. When the coil turns off, the diode conducts and clamps the voltage.

**Common mistakes**:
• Reversing polarity (band on the wrong side).  
• Under-rating reverse voltage or current.  
• Ignoring heat from V_forward at high current.  
• Using a slow diode where fast switching is needed.

**Why it matters**:
Prevents voltage spikes, guards against wiring errors, and turns alternating current into direct current in simple supplies.

**Related**: Light-emitting diode.

**Bottom line**: Point the diode the right way, meet reverse-voltage and current ratings, and verify power dissipation.

label: Light-Emitting Diode (LED)
description:
**What it is**: A <node id="28">diode</node> that emits light when forward-biased. It needs a current-limiting element (usually a resistor). Used as indicators and simple visual feedback.

**How it behaves**:
• Has a forward voltage (approx.): red ≈ 1.8–2.2 V, green ≈ 2.0–3.0 V, blue/white ≈ 2.7–3.3 V (varies by part and current).  
• Brightness scales with current; exceeding the rated current overheats and kills the device.  
• Very low reverse-voltage rating—do not reverse-bias.

**How to use it**:
• Put a resistor in series to set current: R = (V_supply − V_forward) / I_target.  
• Check power in the resistor (I²·R) and in the LED (≈ I · V_forward).  
• Observe polarity: anode to positive, cathode to negative (flat edge or shorter lead is usually the cathode; check footprint pin-1/marking).  
• Driving from a microcontroller: ensure the pin’s current limit isn’t exceeded; use a transistor if higher current is needed.  
• For dimming, use pulse-width modulation rather than running continuously at low current.

**Example in practice**:
From 3.3 V with a red LED (V_forward ≈ 2.0 V) at 8 mA: R ≈ (3.3 − 2.0)/0.008 = 162.5 Ω → choose 160 Ω or 180 Ω.  
Resistor power ≈ 0.008²·160 ≈ 0.010 W → a 0.125 W part is fine.

**Common mistakes**:
• No series resistor (or too small) → overcurrent and failure.  
• Wrong polarity; placing the resistor far from the LED.  
• Exceeding microcontroller pin current limits.

**Why it matters**:
Clear visual status with minimal cost; teaches current limiting and polarity discipline used everywhere. Leads to more advanced topics in Semiconductors such as band-gap and optics.

**Bottom line**: Always use a series resistor, get polarity right, and verify current and power are within limits.

label: Capacitor — Electrolytic / Polymer
description:
**What it is**: A polarized, higher-value capacitor used for bulk energy storage and smoothing on power rails. Polymer types handle ripple better than traditional electrolytics.

**How it behaves**:
• Stores charge: Q = C·V; large C smooths slow changes in current and voltage.  
• Has internal resistance and inductance; good for low-to-mid frequencies, not fast edges.  
• Polarized: reversing it can damage the part (check +/− markings).  
• Limited lifetime (electrolytic dries out); polymer parts have better ripple and life.

**How to use it**:
• Place near regulators and loads to reduce ripple and hold-up during steps.  
• Choose voltage rating with comfortable margin (≈2× the rail).  
• Check ripple current rating and temperature; ensure the part can handle expected ripple.  
• Pair with small ceramic capacitors for fast edges; the ceramic handles high-frequency noise.

**Example in practice**:
On a 5 V rail drawing up to 300 mA with 100 mA load steps, place a 47–220 µF electrolytic near the regulator output and add a 4.7–10 µF ceramic nearby for mid/high-frequency support.

**Common mistakes**:
• Reversed polarity or voltage rating too close to the rail.  
• Using only electrolytics for decoupling fast digital chips.  
• Ignoring ripple current and temperature—shortened life.

**Why it matters**:
Keeps rails stable during load changes and reduces visible ripple; essential for reliable power.

**Bottom line**: Use polarized bulk capacitors for smoothing and hold-up, with enough voltage and ripple margin, and pair them with small ceramics for fast transients.

label: MOSFET — N-Channel
description:
**What it is**: Metal Oxide Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor. Functionally, it acts as a voltage-controlled switch. With gate driven by logic (3.3/5 V), it can turn loads on and off efficiently.

**How it behaves**:
• Gate voltage controls channel resistance; aim for a low on-resistance when fully enhanced.  
• Threshold voltage is not the operating point; you need higher gate voltage than threshold for low loss.  
• Has a body diode from source to drain; affects polarity and protection.

**How to use it (low-side switch)**:
• Source to ground, drain to load, other side of load to supply; drive gate from a microcontroller or driver.  
• Verify the part reaches low on-resistance at your gate voltage (e.g., ≤100 mΩ at 3.3 V for modest currents).  
• Add a gate resistor (10–100 Ω) to tame ringing; ensure a defined off state (pull-down).  
• For inductive loads, add a diode across the load (flyback path).

**Example in practice**:
Switch a 12 V, 500 mA load from a 3.3 V microcontroller: choose a logic-level MOSFET specified with low on-resistance at V_gate = 3.3 V; estimate loss P ≈ I²·R_on = 0.5²·0.05 = 0.125 W → check package thermal limits.

**Common mistakes**:
• Picking by threshold voltage instead of on-resistance at the actual gate drive.  
• Forgetting the body diode orientation; using high-side without a proper gate driver.  
• No flyback diode on inductive loads.

**Why it matters**:
Provides efficient, cool switching for LEDs, motors, heaters, and power rails under logic control.

**Bottom line**: Ensure the MOSFET is truly logic-level at your gate voltage, check power loss, and add proper protection for inductive loads.

label: Kirchhoff’s Current Law
description:
**What it is**: At any node, the algebraic sum of currents is zero (current that leaves equals current that enters).

**How to use it**:
• Choose current directions; write a sum = 0 for the node.  
• Detect floating nodes and missing return paths during schematic review.

**Example**:
Three branches at a node: I1 (leaving), I2 (leaving), I3 (entering). Sum: I1 + I2 − I3 = 0 → solve the unknown.

**Relevance**:
• Fastest way to spot “no return path” bugs before a board spin.  
• Validates sensor and bias networks so inputs aren’t left floating.  
• Turns messy schematics into solvable equations quickly.

**Common mistakes**:
• Mixing sign conventions mid-solution.  
• Assuming a ground symbol guarantees a physical return path.

**Bottom line**: Use node sums to answer “where does the current go?”—it exposes missing or wrong connections immediately.

label: Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law
description:
**What it is**: Around any closed loop, the algebraic sum of voltage drops is zero.

**How to use it**:
• Mark polarities; walk a loop and sum signed drops = 0.  
• Catch impossible extra volts or missing connections.

**Example**:
Supply 5 V feeds R1 then R2 back to ground. Loop: +5 − V_R1 − V_R2 = 0 → solve drops and verify they add to 5 V.

**Relevance**:
• Exposes wiring mistakes that pass visual inspection.  
• Confirms regulator or battery headroom across real paths.  
• Anchors bring-up: measured drops must close the loop.

**Common mistakes**:
• Flipping polarity mid-loop.  
• Ignoring source internal resistance when drops don’t add up.

**Bottom line**: Loop sums verify consistency and catch bad nets before you burn time on layout.

label: Impedance
description:
**What it is**: The <node id="40">AC</node> generalization of <node id="34">resistance</node>. Impedance (Z) combines real resistance (R) and frequency-dependent reactance (X) from capacitors/inductors: Z = R + jX. Magnitude |Z| and phase θ tell you how much a signal is reduced and time-shifted.

**Key relations**:
• Capacitor: X_C = −1/(2π f C)  → higher f ⇒ lower |X_C|  
• Inductor:  X_L =  2π f L      → higher f ⇒ higher |X_L|  
• Ohm’s law (AC/phasor): V = I·Z;  |V| = |I|·|Z|, phase(V) = phase(I) + θ  
• Series: Z_total = Z1 + Z2 + …  
• Parallel: use admittance Y = 1/Z;  Y_total = Σ(1/Zi), then Z_total = 1/Y_total

**How to use**:
• Size/verify parts at the **frequencies that matter** (switching edges, clock harmonics).  
• Choose capacitors/inductors by where their reactance places your pole/zero or how low |Z| is in the band of interest.  
• For decoupling, aim for **low |Z| vs f** at the IC’s current-spike spectrum; placement (low ESL) matters as much as value.

**Example**:
At 10 MHz, a 0.1 µF ceramic: |X_C| ≈ 1/(2π·10e6·0.1e−6) ≈ 0.16 Ω (ignoring ESR/ESL). It shunts HF current well; an electrolytic of the same value won’t (its ESL makes it inductive here).

**Common mistakes**:
• Treating all parts as pure R at all frequencies.  
• Adding big value caps far away and expecting good HF decoupling.  
• Ignoring phase—loop stability and signal integrity depend on it.

**Relevance**:
Impedance is the language of real PCBs. It explains ringing, crosstalk, decoupling, stability, EMI, and why layout beats ideal math.

**Bottom line**: Think in Z, not just R. Compute/estimate Z where your signals live, and place parts to keep **the right impedance in the right band**.

label: Alternating Current
description:
**What it is**: Current and voltage that **periodically reverse direction**. Typically modeled as sinusoids: v(t) = V̂·sin(2πft + φ), i(t) = Î·sin(2πft + φ). 

 Key terms: **frequency** f (Hz), **period** T = 1/f, **phase** φ, **RMS** (V_RMS = V̂/√2 for a sine).

**Why it matters (Relevance)**:
• Most real signals are not DC—edges and ripple have frequency content.  
• Power systems (50/60 Hz) and many sensors/communications are AC.  
• AC thinking unlocks **impedance**, **filters**, **stability**, and **signal integrity**.

**Key relations**:
• Capacitor reactance: X_C = −1/(2πfC) → higher f ⇒ lower |X_C|.  
• Inductor reactance: X_L = 2πfL → higher f ⇒ higher |X_L|.  
• Phasor Ohm’s law: V = I·Z, where Z = R + jX (impedance).  
• Power (sinusoidal, linear loads): P = V_RMS·I_RMS·cosφ (real),  Q = V_RMS·I_RMS·sinφ (reactive),  S = V_RMS·I_RMS (apparent).

**How to use**:
• Work in **RMS** for heating and sizing; use **peak** for headroom (e.g., 120 VAC_RMS ≈ 170 V_peak).  
• Evaluate parts at the **frequencies that matter**: compute X_C/X_L and use Z for drops and currents.  
• For decoupling and fast digital edges, assume significant high-frequency content—choose components/placement to keep **|Z| low** near those bands.

**Example**:
A 0.1 µF ceramic at 10 MHz has |X_C| ≈ 0.16 Ω (ignoring ESR/ESL) → excellent shunt for HF spikes; a bulk electrolytic has higher ESL and looks inductive here.

**Common mistakes**:
• Treating AC like DC (ignoring reactance/phase).  
• Mixing RMS and peak values.  
• Expecting a distant, large capacitor to fix high-frequency noise.

**Bottom line**: AC introduces **frequency and phase**. Think in **impedance vs frequency** and size/locate parts for the band your circuit actually uses.

label: Bandgap
description:
**What it is**: The energy difference (E_g) between a semiconductor’s valence and conduction bands. In **direct-bandgap** materials (e.g., InGaN, GaAsP), electron–hole recombination can emit a photon with energy ≈ E_g. Silicon is **indirect** bandgap → inefficient light emission.

**Key relations**:
• Photon wavelength: λ ≈ h·c / E_g  
• Forward voltage correlation: q·V_f ≈ E_g (first-order; real V_f also includes series resistance and recombination effects).  
• Temperature: E_g ↓ as T ↑ → V_f typically drops with temperature.

**How to use**:
• Expect higher E_g → shorter λ (bluer light) and generally higher LED V_f.  
• White LEDs: blue/UV die + phosphor; electrical V_f tracks the blue die’s E_g.  
• Use E_g→λ to sanity-check color vs expected V_f before sizing current-limit resistors.

**Relevance**:
Explains why red/amber LEDs run near ~2 V while blue/white sit closer to ~3 V, and why silicon diodes don’t make efficient LEDs.

**Common mistakes**:
• Treating q·V_f = E_g as exact.  
• Assuming any diode emits light.  
• Ignoring temperature drift of V_f/brightness.

**Bottom line**: Bandgap sets photon energy and strongly influences LED color and forward voltage—plan drive and headroom accordingly.

label: Semiconductor
description:
**What it is**: A class of materials (e.g., Si, GaAs, GaN) whose conductivity sits between conductors and insulators and can be tuned by doping, electric fields, temperature, and light.

**Key ideas**:
• **Carriers**: electrons (n-type) and holes (p-type); density and mobility set conductivity.  
• **Doping**: donors/acceptors set n or p behavior; profiles create device regions.  
• **<node id="41">Bandgap</node> (E_g)**: energy gap controls intrinsic carriers, leakage, and (for direct bandgaps) light emission.  
• **Junctions & fields**: p–n junctions make depletion regions; electric fields modulate channels (MOSFETs).

**How to use (intuition for circuits)**:
• Diodes = one p–n junction → rectification, forward drop, reverse breakdown.  
• LEDs = direct-bandgap junctions → photons ~ E_g.  
• MOSFETs = field-controlled channels + a body diode → low-loss switching if gate is driven correctly.

**Relevance**:
Explains forward voltage, leakage, temperature drift, body diodes, ESD structures, and why devices are not ideal switches.

**Common mistakes**:
• Treating V_th (MOSFET) as a usable gate voltage.  
• Assuming all diodes emit light efficiently.  
• Ignoring temperature effects on leakage and V_f.

**Bottom line**: Semiconductors are **tunable conductors**. Devices work by shaping carrier densities and electric fields—this underlies diodes, LEDs, and transistors.

label: Buck Converter
description:
**What it is**: A switching DC-DC converter that **steps a higher DC voltage down** to a lower DC voltage using a pulsed inductor.

**How it works (ideal)**:
• Switch (MOSFET) connects Vin to the inductor for duty **D** → current ramps up; average **Vout ≈ D·Vin**.  
• Switch opens for (1−D) → inductor current freewheels through a diode/low-side MOSFET.  
• Output capacitor supplies ripple current; input ceramic caps tame the hot loop.

**Core relations**:
• Duty (CCM): **Vout ≈ D·Vin**.  
• Inductor ripple: **ΔI_L ≈ (Vin − Vout)·D / (L·f_s)**.  
• Output ripple (ideal): **ΔV_out ≈ ΔI_L / (8·f_s·C)** plus **ΔV_ESR ≈ ΔI_L·ESR**.

**Sizing quickstart**:
• Choose **ΔI_L ≈ 20–40% of I_out** → solve **L**.  
• Pick **C** for ripple target (include ESR at switching frequency).  
• Select diode/synchronous FET with real voltage/current/thermal margin.  
• Higher **f_s** → smaller L/C but more switching loss/EMI.

**Layout must-dos**:
• Minimize the **hot loop** (VIN cap → switch → diode/low-side → GND → VIN cap). Place the **input ceramic at the switch pin**.  
• Keep the switch node short/wide; keep FB trace quiet and away from the switch node; solid ground plane.

**Modes**:
• **CCM**: continuous inductor current, lower ripple (typical at moderate/high load).  
• **DCM**: discontinuous at light load; efficiency control features may change dynamics.

**Example — why not linear? (12 V → 5 V @ 0.6 A)**:
• Load power: **P_out = 3.0 W**.  
• **Linear regulator loss**: (12−5)·0.6 = **4.2 W** heat (~42% efficient).  
• **Buck @ 90%**: P_in ≈ 3.0/0.90 = 3.33 W → **0.33 W** loss (cool, compact).

**Relevance**: Efficient point-of-load generation for logic rails (e.g., 12→5 V, 5→3.3 V) with 85–95%+ efficiency when sized and laid out correctly.

**Common mistakes**:
• Skipping the **input ceramic at the switch** → ringing/EMI/fail.  
• Under-rating FET/diode or ignoring thermal rise.  
• Treating ESR as zero in ripple estimates.

**Bottom line**: Set **L** from current ripple, **C** from voltage ripple (incl. ESR), pick switch/diode with margin, and **win the layout**—that’s where buck designs succeed or fail.
